source.value: What expression is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int_\limits{C} \dfrac{x}{y} \: \textrm{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $x^2 + 16y^2 = 16,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

decisions.question: e-9460

source.question: e-9460
source.value:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{4^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{1^2} = 1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle 4\cos{t}, \: \sin{t} \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \lt 2\pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x}{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=4\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

source.value:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{2^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{3^2} = 1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 3\sin{t} \right\rangle, \qquad -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = 2xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{y^2}{2^2}  = 1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle \cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad \dfrac{\pi}{2} \le t \le \pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{3{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = 12xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =12\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t=24\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}12xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }24\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =24{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+3\cos^2 {t},$ $\textrm d u=-6\sin t\cos 
 t\,\textrm d t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}24{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =-4{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}({4}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}(8-1) \\  & =-\frac{56}{3}\end{aligned}
$$
